items.name: Wheat
items.note: Wheat covers more land than any other food crop on Earth.

items.name: Durum Wheat
items.note: A hard wheat with high protein: the only wheat allowed in Italian dried pasta.

items.name: Rye
items.note: Rye tolerates cold, poor soils, which is why rye bread dominates Northern and Eastern Europe.

items.name: Barley
items.note: About a third of barley is malted for beer and whisky; most of the rest feeds animals.

items.name: Corn
items.note: Maize was bred by Indigenous Mexicans from a wild grass called teosinte with tiny, hard kernels.

items.name: Paddy Rice
items.note: Rice feeds more than half of humanity. "Paddy" is rice still in its inedible husk.

items.name: Buckwheat
items.note: Not wheat at all: buckwheat is a relative of rhubarb and sorrel.

items.name: Teff
items.note: Teff seeds are so tiny that 150 of them weigh as much as one wheat kernel.

items.name: Hay
items.note: A dairy cow eats roughly 25 kg of hay or silage per day.

items.name: Potato
items.note: There are over 4,000 native potato varieties in the Andes.

items.name: Cassava
items.note: Raw cassava contains cyanide compounds; it must be peeled, soaked and cooked to be safe.

items.name: Carrot
items.note: Orange carrots became popular in the 17th-century Netherlands.

items.name: Sugar Beet
items.note: Developed after a chemist found the same sugar as in cane inside beets. Today ~20% of world sugar comes from beet.

items.name: Tomato
items.note: Europeans long thought tomatoes were poisonous; they only entered Italian cooking in the late 1600s.

items.name: Chili Pepper
items.note: Chili reached Asia only in the 1500s via Portuguese traders. Thai and Sichuan food had no chili before that.

items.name: Wasabi
items.note: Real wasabi takes 18 months to grow; most "wasabi" outside Japan is dyed horseradish.

items.name: Soybeans
items.note: About 77% of the world’s soy is fed to livestock; only ~7% is eaten directly as tofu, soy milk and similar.

items.name: Peanuts
items.note: Peanuts are legumes, not nuts: the pods ripen underground.

items.name: Sesame Seeds
items.note: One of the oldest oilseed crops: grown in the Indus Valley 5,000 years ago.

items.name: Hops
items.note: Hops add bitterness and preserve beer; they were adopted by German brewers around 800 CE.

items.name: Saffron Crocus Flowers
items.note: Each crocus flower gives only 3 threads; about 150,000 flowers make one kilogram of saffron.

items.name: Apple
items.note: Every apple tree grown from seed is genetically unique; named varieties are all grafted clones.

items.name: Wine Grapes
items.note: The oldest evidence of winemaking comes from 8,000-year-old clay jars in Georgia.

items.name: Olives
items.note: Fresh olives are inedibly bitter; they must be cured in brine, salt or lye first.

items.name: Orange
items.note: Brazil and the USA grow most of the world’s orange juice; oranges came to the Americas with Columbus.

items.name: Almonds
items.note: California grows ~80% of the world’s almonds, and pollinating them needs most of the USA’s commercial beehives.

items.name: Pine Nuts
items.note: Pine cones take up to three years to mature, which is why pine nuts are so expensive.

items.name: Sichuan Peppercorns
items.note: Sichuan pepper causes a tingling numbness called "má" thanks to the molecule hydroxy-alpha-sanshool.

items.name: Sugarcane
items.note: Cane sugar drove the Atlantic slave trade: most enslaved Africans were taken to work on sugar plantations.

items.name: Banana
items.note: Nearly all export bananas are one clone, the Cavendish, so a single disease can threaten the whole crop.

items.name: Avocado
items.note: One avocado needs on average ~70 litres of water to grow.

items.name: Oil Palm Fruit
items.note: Palm oil is the most-used vegetable oil on Earth and is in roughly half of all packaged supermarket products.

items.name: Cashew Nuts
items.note: Cashews grow out of the bottom of a fruit, and their shells contain a skin-burning oil related to poison ivy.

items.name: Cocoa Pods
items.note: About 60% of the world’s cocoa comes from just two countries: Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, mostly from small family farms.

items.name: Coffee Cherries
items.note: Each coffee cherry holds two seeds: the coffee "beans". A tree yields only about 0.5 kg of roasted coffee a year.

items.name: Tea Leaves
items.note: Green, black, oolong and white tea all come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis.

items.name: Vanilla Pods
items.note: Outside Mexico vanilla flowers must be pollinated by hand, one by one, a method found by 12-year-old Edmond Albius in 1841.

items.name: Pepper Berries
items.note: Black, white and green pepper all come from the same vine; the difference is when and how they are processed.

items.name: Cinnamon Bark
items.note: Cinnamon is the inner bark of a tree, peeled by hand and rolled into quills.

items.name: Nutmeg Fruit
items.note: In 1667 the Dutch traded Manhattan to the English for Run, a tiny nutmeg island.

items.name: Button Mushrooms
items.note: Button, cremini and portobello mushrooms are the same species at different ages.

items.name: Porcini
items.note: Porcini cannot be farmed: they live in symbiosis with the roots of living trees.

items.name: Black Truffle
items.note: Truffles grow underground and are found by trained dogs or pigs.

items.name: Juniper Berries
items.note: Juniper "berries" are actually tiny cones. They flavour gin and sauerkraut.

items.name: Maple Sap
items.note: It takes about 40 litres of maple sap to boil down one litre of maple syrup.

items.name: Water
items.note: Producing 1 kg of beef uses around 15,000 litres of water, mostly to grow feed.

items.name: Salt
items.note: Salt was so valuable in the ancient world that Roman soldiers were sometimes paid with it; "salary" comes from sal.

items.name: Nigari
items.note: Nigari (magnesium chloride) is what is left after salt crystallises from seawater. It sets soy milk into tofu.

items.name: Rock Salt
items.note: Most table salt comes from mines in ancient seabeds, not from today’s oceans.

items.name: Trona
items.note: Most of America’s baking soda comes from trona, a mineral left by a lake that evaporated 50 million years ago.

items.name: Cow Milk
items.note: A dairy cow must have a calf every year or so to keep producing milk.

items.name: Water Buffalo Milk
items.note: Authentic mozzarella di bufala is made from water buffalo milk.

items.name: Cattle
items.note: A beef steer eats about 6–8 kg of feed for every 1 kg of weight it gains.

items.name: Calf
items.note: Traditional rennet for cheese is an enzyme from the stomach of young calves.

items.name: Broiler Chicken
items.note: There are more chickens on Earth than all other birds combined: over 20 billion at any time.

items.name: Honey
items.note: A bee makes about 1/12 teaspoon of honey in its whole life; one jar needs ~2 million flower visits.

items.name: Cod
items.note: Cod fueled Europe for centuries; the Grand Banks fishery collapsed from overfishing in 1992.

items.name: Anchovies
items.note: Most of the world’s anchovy catch is ground into fish meal to feed farmed fish, pigs and chickens.

items.name: Eel
items.note: Nobody has ever bred European eels in captivity; all farmed eels are caught as wild babies.

items.name: Nori Seaweed
items.note: Nori farming only became possible after British scientist Kathleen Drew-Baker discovered its life cycle in 1949.

items.name: Wheat Flour
items.note: White flour is made by removing the bran and germ, which is where most fibre and vitamins are.

items.name: Semolina
items.note: Semolina is coarsely ground durum wheat; its strong gluten keeps pasta firm when boiled.

items.name: White Rice
items.note: Polishing rice removes the bran. Brown rice keeps it and is more nutritious, but spoils faster.

items.name: Bulgur
items.note: Bulgur is wheat that is parboiled, dried and cracked, so it cooks in minutes.

items.name: Tapioca Starch
items.note: Tapioca is extracted from cassava root; washing it removes the toxic cyanide compounds.

items.name: Nixtamalized Corn
items.note: Nixtamalization (cooking maize in limewater) unlocks niacin. Europeans who adopted corn without it suffered pellagra epidemics.

items.name: Panko
items.note: Panko is made from crustless bread baked with electric current, which gives its airy flakes.

items.name: Animal Feed
items.note: Compound feed is mostly maize and soybean meal. Producing animal feed uses about a third of the world’s cropland.

items.name: Olive Oil
items.note: It takes about 5 kg of olives to make one litre of extra virgin olive oil.

items.name: Soybean Oil
items.note: Crushing soybeans gives ~20% oil and ~80% protein-rich meal, which mostly becomes animal feed.

items.name: Almond Milk
items.note: One glass of almond milk can contain fewer than 5 almonds.

items.name: Tofu
items.note: Tofu is made like cheese: soy milk is curdled with nigari or gypsum, then pressed.

items.name: Butter
items.note: Making 1 kg of butter takes about 22 litres of milk.

items.name: Yogurt
items.note: Yogurt bacteria turn milk sugar (lactose) into lactic acid, which thickens and preserves the milk.

items.name: Cheddar
items.note: About 10 litres of milk make 1 kg of hard cheese; the rest becomes whey.

items.name: Parmesan
items.note: Parmigiano Reggiano is aged at least 12 months, often 24–36. Its whey is fed to the pigs that become Parma ham.

items.name: Ricotta
items.note: Ricotta means "re-cooked": it is made by reheating the whey left over from other cheeses.

items.name: Emmental
items.note: The holes in Emmental are CO₂ bubbles made by Propionibacterium during ripening.

items.name: Beef Steak
items.note: Only about 40% of a live steer’s weight ends up as retail meat.

items.name: Pork Chop
items.note: Butchers say you can use every part of the pig "except the squeal", including intestines as sausage casings.

items.name: Gelatin
items.note: Gelatin is collagen boiled out of animal bones and skin. Gummy bears and panna cotta both rely on it.

items.name: Prosciutto
items.note: Prosciutto di Parma is cured with nothing but sea salt and air for at least 12 months.

items.name: Katsuobushi
items.note: Katsuobushi is skipjack tuna simmered, smoked and fermented with mould for months until hard as wood. It is the backbone of Japanese dashi.

items.name: Salt Cod
items.note: Salted cod (bacalhau) let Basque and Portuguese sailors carry protein across oceans for months.

items.name: Fish Meal
items.note: Farmed salmon need fish meal and fish oil; it has taken up to 3 kg of wild fish to raise 1 kg of salmon.

items.name: Surimi
items.note: Surimi is fish paste. "Crab sticks" are usually surimi made from Alaska pollock, not crab.

items.name: Black Peppercorns
items.note: Black pepper is unripe pepper berries left to dry and blacken in the sun.

items.name: White Peppercorns
items.note: White pepper is ripe pepper berries soaked until the skin rots off, leaving the white seed.

items.name: Nutmeg
items.note: One fruit gives two spices: the seed is nutmeg and its red lacy coating is mace.

items.name: Cured Vanilla Beans
items.note: Green vanilla has no aroma. Curing — scalding, sweating and slow drying — takes 3–6 months and develops vanillin.

items.name: Saffron Threads
items.note: Saffron is the world’s most expensive spice by weight because every stigma is picked by hand.

items.name: Curry Powder
items.note: "Curry powder" was invented by British merchants to imitate Indian spice mixes, which cooks in India blend fresh for each dish.

items.name: Ras el Hanout
items.note: Ras el hanout means "head of the shop": the best spices a merchant has. Some blends contain 30 ingredients.

items.name: White Sugar
items.note: Refined cane and beet sugar are chemically identical: pure sucrose.

items.name: Fermented Cocoa Beans
items.note: Cocoa beans are fermented for about a week under banana leaves; without this step chocolate has no chocolate flavour.

items.name: Cocoa Mass
items.note: Ground cocoa nibs melt into a liquid paste called cocoa liquor (no alcohol involved).

items.name: Dark Chocolate
items.note: Conching — stirring liquid chocolate for hours or days — was invented by Rodolphe Lindt in Bern in 1879.

items.name: Milk Chocolate
items.note: Milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland by Daniel Peter in 1875 using Henri Nestlé’s milk powder.

items.name: Green Coffee Beans
items.note: Coffee cherries are pulped, fermented, washed and dried before the green beans are ever roasted.

items.name: Matcha
items.note: Matcha tea plants are shaded for weeks before harvest, then the leaves are stone-ground: about 40 g per hour.

items.name: Hazelnut Cocoa Spread
items.note: Popular hazelnut spreads are over 50% sugar, about 20% palm oil and around 13% hazelnuts.

items.name: Malted Barley
items.note: Malting lets barley sprout so its enzymes turn starch into fermentable sugar, then kiln-dries it.

items.name: Red Wine
items.note: Cream of tartar, a key part of baking powder, crystallises on the inside of wine barrels.

items.name: Yeast
items.note: Commercial baker’s yeast is grown in huge tanks fed on sugar-beet or cane molasses.

items.name: Koji
items.note: Koji is rice grown with the mould Aspergillus oryzae, Japan’s "national fungus". It powers soy sauce, miso, sake and mirin.

items.name: Soy Sauce
items.note: Traditional soy sauce ferments for 6 months to several years.

items.name: Fish Sauce
items.note: Fish sauce is anchovies and salt fermented for a year or more. Ancient Romans loved a similar sauce called garum.

items.name: Balsamic Vinegar
items.note: Traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena is boiled grape must aged at least 12 years in a series of wooden barrels.

items.name: Worcestershire Sauce
items.note: Worcestershire sauce contains fermented anchovies and tamarind from India.

items.name: Orange Marmalade
items.note: True marmalade uses bitter Seville oranges, which are almost inedible raw.

items.name: Red Bean Paste
items.note: Sweet red bean paste (anko) fills mochi, mooncakes, dorayaki and taiyaki across East Asia.

items.name: Do Chua Pickles
items.note: Vietnamese pickled carrot and daikon, the crunch inside a bánh mì.

items.name: Dashi
items.note: Dashi’s savoury depth comes from glutamate (kombu) plus inosinate (katsuobushi): the discovery of umami in 1908.

items.name: Bolognese Ragù
items.note: The official 1982 Bologna ragù recipe uses only a little tomato, plus milk and wine, and is simmered for hours.

items.name: Mole Sauce
items.note: Mole poblano can contain over 20 ingredients, including several kinds of dried chili, chocolate, nuts, seeds and spices.

items.name: Ramen Noodles
items.note: Ramen noodles get their springy bite and yellow colour from kansui, an alkaline mineral water.

items.name: Baguette
items.note: By French law a "baguette de tradition" may contain only flour, water, salt and yeast or leaven.

items.name: Injera
items.note: Injera batter is fermented for days, giving the spongy, sour Ethiopian flatbread its bubbles.

items.name: Puff Pastry
items.note: Classic puff pastry has 729 layers of butter and dough from six "turns".

items.name: Marzipan
items.note: Marzipan came to Europe from Persia via the Arab world; Lübeck in Germany is still famous for it.

items.name: Baking Soda
items.note: Baking soda is mined as trona or made by the Solvay process from salt and limestone.

items.name: Baking Powder
items.note: Baking powder is a ready-mixed acid (often cream of tartar from winemaking) and base (baking soda).

items.name: Slaked Lime
items.note: Food-grade lime (cal) is used in Mexico to nixtamalize corn for tortillas.

items.name: Lye
items.note: German pretzels get their dark, shiny crust from a dip in a lye solution before baking.

items.name: Bircher Muesli
items.note: Invented around 1900 by Swiss doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner.

items.name: Fish and Chips
items.note: Traditionally fried in beef dripping.

items.name: Croissants
items.note: Croissants descend from the Austrian kipferl, brought to Paris in the 1830s.

items.name: Pizza Margherita
items.note: Named in 1889 after Queen Margherita: tomato, mozzarella and basil echo the Italian flag.

items.name: Pastel de Nata
items.note: Created by monks of the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon, who used egg whites to starch their clothes.

items.name: Chicken Tikka Masala
items.note: Widely said to have been invented in Glasgow in the 1970s.

items.name: Pork Vindaloo
items.note: From Goa; the name comes from the Portuguese "carne de vinha d’alhos": meat in wine-vinegar and garlic.

items.name: Xiaolongbao
items.note: The soup inside is jellied pork broth that melts when steamed.

items.name: California Roll
items.note: Invented in Los Angeles (or Vancouver) to win over diners wary of raw fish.

items.name: Bánh Mì
items.note: A fusion born of French colonial baguettes and Vietnamese fillings.

items.name: Tacos al Pastor
items.note: Brought to Mexico by Lebanese immigrants, who adapted shawarma.

items.name: Lomo Saltado
items.note: Peruvian-Chinese "chifa" cooking: a wok stir-fry with soy sauce and fries.

items.name: Chocolate Chip Cookies
items.note: Invented by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn, Massachusetts, around 1938.

items.name: Caesar Salad
items.note: Created by Italian immigrant Caesar Cardini in Tijuana, Mexico, in 1924.

items.name: Cheese Fondue
items.note: Promoted as the Swiss national dish by the Swiss Cheese Union in the 1930s.

items.name: Doro Wat
items.note: Ethiopian chicken stew, simmered for hours with a dozen spices and eaten with teff injera.

items.name: Peach Melba
items.note: Created by Auguste Escoffier for the opera singer Nellie Melba.

items.name: Capuns
items.note: A Graubünden specialty: spätzle dough and dried meat wrapped in chard leaves.

buildings.name: Field
buildings.desc: Grows annual crops: grains, vegetables, legumes, herbs. Seed cost is paid each cycle.

buildings.name: Orchard
buildings.desc: Fruit trees, nut trees, berry bushes and vines. Slow, but valuable.

buildings.name: Tropical Greenhouse
buildings.desc: Heated glasshouse for tropical crops: cocoa, coffee, vanilla, spices, bananas. In reality these are imported from the tropics.

buildings.name: Mushroom Cellar
buildings.desc: Dark, humid cellar for cultivated mushrooms.

buildings.name: Forager's Lodge
buildings.desc: Gathers wild foods from the forest: truffles, porcini, maple sap, berries. Must be next to forest.

buildings.name: Pasture & Barn
buildings.desc: Cattle, sheep, goats and water buffalo. Grazing animals eat hay.

buildings.name: Pigsty
buildings.desc: Raises pigs on animal feed.

buildings.name: Poultry House
buildings.desc: Chickens, ducks, turkeys, geese, quail and rabbits.

buildings.name: Apiary
buildings.desc: Beehives. Bees need flowers: honey is produced from nectar.

buildings.name: Aquaculture Pens
buildings.desc: Farmed fish and shellfish. Carnivorous fish like salmon eat fish meal made from wild fish.

buildings.name: Well
buildings.desc: Draws fresh water. Almost every recipe needs it.

buildings.name: Salt Pans
buildings.desc: Evaporates seawater in the sun to harvest salt. Must touch water.

buildings.name: Quarry & Mine
buildings.desc: Mines rock salt, limestone and trona. Must touch rocky ground.

buildings.name: Fishing Dock
buildings.desc: Boats catch wild fish, shellfish and seaweed. Must touch water.

buildings.name: Mill
buildings.desc: Mills grains into flour, polishes rice, makes starches.

buildings.name: Feed Mill
buildings.desc: Mixes compound animal feed. Most of the world’s soy and maize ends up here.

buildings.name: Press House
buildings.desc: Presses oils and juices; makes plant milks and tofu.

buildings.name: Creamery
buildings.desc: Separates cream, churns butter, makes yogurt and cheese.

buildings.name: Butchery
buildings.desc: Breaks animals down into cuts, fat and bones.

buildings.name: Smokehouse & Curing
buildings.desc: Cures, dries and smokes meat and fish.

buildings.name: Fish Processing
buildings.desc: Fillets fish, peels shrimp, salts and cans seafood.

buildings.name: Spice Mill
buildings.desc: Dries, cures, grinds and blends spices and herbs.

buildings.name: Sugar Refinery
buildings.desc: Refines cane and beet into sugars and syrups.

buildings.name: Roastery
buildings.desc: Ferments, roasts and grinds cocoa, coffee, tea and nuts. Makes chocolate.

buildings.name: Brewery & Winery
buildings.desc: Malts, brews, ferments wine and distills spirits.

buildings.name: Fermentation Cellar
buildings.desc: Yeast, koji, soy sauce, miso, vinegars, pickles and kimchi.

buildings.name: Preserves & Cannery
buildings.desc: Jams, dried fruit, tomato products and other preserves.

buildings.name: Sauce & Prep Kitchen
buildings.desc: Stocks, mother sauces, pastes and prepared bases.

buildings.name: Pasta & Noodle Workshop
buildings.desc: Pasta, noodles, tortillas and wrappers.

buildings.name: Bakery
buildings.desc: Breads, doughs and pastry bases.

buildings.name: Pâtisserie
buildings.desc: Creams, custards, sponges and confectionery.

buildings.name: Mineral Works
buildings.desc: Refines salt, makes baking soda, baking powder, slaked lime and lye.

buildings.name: Kitchen
buildings.desc: Cooks dishes you have discovered. Discover new dishes in the Test Kitchen.

buildings.name: Farmhouse
buildings.desc: Your headquarters and central warehouse. Everything you produce is stored here.
